{{Short description|Prime integer calculated using a primality-proving algorithm}}
{{distinguish|Probable prime}}
In [[number theory]], a '''provable prime''' is an [[integer]] that has been calculated to be [[prime number|prime]] using a primality-proving [[algorithm]]. Boot-strapping techniques using [[Pocklington primality test]] are the most common ways to generate provable primes for cryptography.<ref>{{citation|title=An Introduction to Fast Generation of Large Prime Numbers|series=Philips Journal of Research|author=C. Couvreur and J. J. Quisquater|volume=37|year=1982|pages=231–264}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1= Crandall |first1= Richard|last2=Pomerance |first2= Carl|date=2005 |title=Prime Numbers: A Computational Perspective |publisher= Springer|isbn=978-0387-25282-7|pages=174–178}}</ref> 
Contrast with [[probable prime]], which is likely (but not certain) to be prime, based on the output of a [[probabilistic algorithm|probabilistic]] [[primality test]]. 

In principle, every prime number can be proved to be prime in [[polynomial time]] by using the [[AKS primality test]]. Other methods which guarantee that their result is prime, but which do not work for all primes, are useful for the random generation of provable primes.<ref>{{citation|title=RSA and Public-Key Cryptography|series=Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications|first=Richard A.|last=Mollin|publisher=CRC Press|year=2002|isbn=9781420035247|pages=124–125|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mZUYNy0UGNUC&pg=PA124}}.</ref>

Provable primes have also been generated on embedded devices.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Christophe|first=Clavier|title=Generating Provable Primes Efficiently on Embedded Devices|url=https://www.iacr.org/archive/pkc2012/72930372/72930372.pdf|journal=The International Association for Cryptologic Research}}</ref>
